items.prompt: In SMART goals, what does the letter M stand for?

options.label: Measurable
Motivating
Monitored
Manageable

rubric: M stands for Measurable: progress can be checked against a clear measure.
Manageable, Motivating and Monitored sound plausible but are not part of the standard acronym.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a regular one-on-one meeting between a manager and a direct report?

options.label: To share company announcements and updates with the whole team
To walk through the team's budget and spending plans in detail
To log formal warnings and track disciplinary steps for the HR file
To give the report space to discuss progress and needs

rubric: One-on-ones exist to support the individual: progress, obstacles, development and concerns.
Distractors describe other meetings (budget, all-hands, disciplinary) that one-on-ones are often mistaken for.

items.prompt: Which definition best describes delegation?

options.label: Handing off unwanted work and staying out of it entirely
Splitting every task into equal parts for everyone
Assigning a task along with the authority to complete it
Doing a task yourself while others watch and learn

rubric: Delegation means assigning a task plus the authority needed to do it.
Dumping unwanted work or equal splitting confuses delegation with offloading or fairness.

items.prompt: In the SBI feedback model, what do the letters stand for?

options.label: Summary, Basis, Insight
Situation, Behavior, Impact
Strength, Blocker, Intent
Skill, Boundary, Improvement

rubric: SBI stands for Situation, Behavior, Impact, which anchors feedback in observable facts.
Other options are invented word combinations that sound like feedback vocabulary.

items.prompt: How often should one-on-ones ideally be held?

options.label: Only when a performance problem comes up
Once a year around review time
Whenever the manager happens to be free
Weekly or biweekly at a set time

rubric: Good practice is a consistent weekly or biweekly rhythm.
Ad hoc or annual meetings make one-on-ones reactive and easy to skip.

items.prompt: Which items belong in a clear expectation when you assign a task? Select all that apply.

options.label: The outcome that is needed
The deadline
The manager's guess about the person's mood
Comments on a coworker's weaknesses
The quality standard expected

rubric: Clear expectations state the outcome, the timing and the quality standard.
Mood guesses and comments about coworkers are not part of task expectations.

items.prompt: Priya, one of your reports, has missed three deadlines this month. You are a new manager and want to address it. According to standard practice, what should you do first?

options.label: Wait for the annual review to raise it with her
Remind the whole team about deadlines
Ask her peers if they have seen the same delays
Meet her privately and give specific examples

rubric: Address issues early, privately and with specific examples.
Public hints, waiting, or polling peers delay or undermine a direct conversation.

items.prompt: Why do managers delegate tasks instead of doing everything themselves?

options.label: It moves responsibility for poor results onto the team members
It lets the manager avoid learning how the work is done
It removes the need to set expectations for the task or check in
It builds team skills and frees time for higher-value work

rubric: Delegation develops people and frees manager capacity.
Distractors treat delegation as blame-shifting or avoidance; accountability and expectations remain.

items.prompt: Which comment is an example of behavior-based feedback?

options.label: The report went out with three wrong totals
You were careless with the report this week, and it showed
You don't seem to care about meeting deadlines lately
Your attitude toward details is hurting the whole team

rubric: Behavior-based feedback describes observable facts, not traits.
The other options judge character with words like always, never, or attitude.

items.prompt: Why should the report usually set much of the agenda in a one-on-one?

options.label: It keeps the meeting shorter for the manager
It prevents any talk about performance
It removes the need for the manager to give feedback
It shows the meeting is for their needs and concerns

rubric: Report-led agendas signal the meeting serves the report and surface real issues.
The manager still gives feedback and discusses performance; distractors misread the idea.

items.prompt: A manager hands over a task saying only, "Sort out the client report." What is the most likely result?

options.label: The work matches the manager's unstated expectations
The person delivers early and needs no guidance
The output may miss what the manager needed
The person feels motivated by total freedom

rubric: Vague instructions leave the person guessing, so results often miss the mark.
Distractors assume the person can read the manager's mind or that vagueness equals trust.

items.prompt: A new hire is doing a task for the first time and has no experience with it. Which management style fits best?

options.label: Directing with explicit steps
Leaving them to work it out alone
Only asking open coaching questions
Delegating fully with no check-ins

rubric: Inexperienced people need clear steps and direction first.
Hands-off or purely questioning styles suit people with more experience.

items.prompt: Why should praise be specific rather than general? Select all that apply.

options.label: It tells the person which behavior to repeat
It shows the manager noticed the actual work
It replaces the need for any developmental feedback
It guarantees a raise at the next review

rubric: Specific praise reinforces the right behavior and shows real attention.
Praise does not replace developmental feedback or promise pay outcomes.

items.prompt: Sam and Lee each believe the other owns the weekly report. Last week it was late, and they snapped at each other in the team chat. You are their manager. What is the best first step?

options.label: Give it to whoever has less work and tell both to move on
Tell them to sort it out themselves or face consequences
Rotate the task weekly without discussing the dispute at all
Talk with each to hear their view, then clarify ownership

rubric: Hearing both sides and then clarifying ownership addresses the root cause.
Ultimatums, silent rotation or quick reassignment leave the unclear ownership and tension unresolved.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a regular one-on-one meeting between a manager and a direct report?

options.label: A private, recurring space focused on the report's needs, progress and obstacles
A formal review session where the manager scores performance against the annual rating
A weekly status report where the manager collects task updates to pass on to senior leaders
A slot used mainly for the manager to hand out new tasks and set the next deadlines

rubric: One-on-ones are a recurring private space for the report's progress, obstacles and development.
Distractors treat it as status reporting, formal rating or task allocation, which crowds out the report's own needs.

items.prompt: Why is the expectation 'respond to customer tickets within 4 working hours' better than 'be responsive'?

options.label: It shows the team that the manager controls how every single task is carried out in detail
It keeps the person's workload constant, since specific targets cannot change once they are set
It removes the need for later feedback because the standard is now fixed and fully settled for good
It lets the person see what good looks like and lets the manager judge the result fairly

rubric: Specific expectations make success visible and assessment fair.
Distractors confuse clarity with removing feedback, controlling methods or freezing workload.

items.prompt: Which example is real delegation rather than just handing off work?

options.label: Forwarding Priya the monthly report template on Friday evening with a note asking her to get it done soon
Giving Priya the monthly report and asking not to be disturbed until it is fully finished, with no check-ins
Giving Priya the monthly report with the outcome, deadline, authority to request data and a mid-point check-in
Telling Priya to complete the monthly report exactly as the manager did last time, with sign-off at every step

rubric: Delegation transfers ownership of an outcome with authority, a deadline and support.
Distractors are vague dumping, step-by-step micromanagement, or abandonment without check-ins.

items.prompt: Which statement is feedback that describes behaviour rather than judging character?

options.label: You have a bad attitude in meetings, and other people have started to notice it
In today's meeting you interrupted Sam three times while he presented the plan
You are rude and dismissive toward colleagues when they present their ideas to the team
You clearly don't respect your teammates' work or their time, and it shows

rubric: Effective feedback names observable behaviour, not traits or motives.
Distractors label character or attitude, which invites defensiveness and gives nothing specific to change.

items.prompt: A manager checks every step of an experienced report's work and rewrites it before it goes out. What is the most likely effect over time?

options.label: The team's workload drops because fewer mistakes reach customers after the rewrites
The report's skills grow faster because every detail is corrected immediately by the manager
The report relies on the manager's approval and takes less ownership of quality
The report trusts the manager more because the work that goes out is always polished

rubric: Micromanaging erodes ownership and creates dependence on the manager.
Distractors assume close correction builds skill, trust or capacity, which it usually does not.

items.prompt: Which are reasons to agree clear goals with a direct report at the start of a period? Select all that apply.

options.label: It guarantees that the report will reach every target set
It removes the need for regular check-ins during the period
It gives both sides a shared basis for later feedback
It helps the report prioritise between competing tasks

rubric: Goals support prioritisation and give a shared basis for feedback.
Goals do not replace check-ins or guarantee results; those are common misconceptions.

items.prompt: Dana, usually talkative, has been silent in team meetings for two weeks, though her output is unchanged. Her manager wonders what is going on. Which response best reflects sound people management?

options.label: Raise it privately in the next one-on-one with open questions, without assuming the cause
Wait until her output drops, since unchanged output means there is nothing yet that needs to be addressed
Call her out in the next team meeting so she knows the silence has been noticed and can explain it
Ask her teammates what they think is wrong and act on the most common view they give

rubric: A private, open conversation checks the cause without assuming it.
Distractors embarrass her publicly, ignore early signals, or rely on gossip instead of asking her.

items.prompt: Leo sent a handover at 5pm instead of noon yesterday, so Mia could not start testing until today. You use situation-behaviour-impact feedback. Which message fits?

options.label: I noticed you seem disorganised lately; maybe you could try managing your time a lot better
Yesterday's handover was a disaster, and I expect you to be much more professional from now on
Leo, yesterday's handover arrived at 5pm, not noon, so Mia couldn't start testing until today
Leo, you were careless with yesterday's handover, and that carelessness held up Mia's testing and the team

rubric: It states the situation, the observable behaviour and the impact without judging character.
Distractors generalise ('always'), label the person, or stay vague about what happened.

items.prompt: A report wants to build stakeholder-presentation skills. Which task is the best to delegate to them?

options.label: Presenting the quarterly project update to stakeholders, with you reviewing the slides beforehand
Sitting in on the stakeholder meeting to take notes and write the summary while you present the update yourself
Preparing all the quarterly slides and data tables on their own while you present the update to stakeholders
Drafting an urgent legal response due within the hour, with nobody available to check it first

rubric: Delegation should match the development goal and include support.
Distractors are filler work, a task with excessive risk and no support, or passive observation.

items.prompt: A report has cancelled the last three one-on-ones, saying they are too busy. What should you do next?

options.label: Keep the meetings but move the topics onto the team meeting agenda so nobody is singled out
Escalate to your own manager that the report is refusing to engage with their line manager
Stop scheduling one-on-ones until they ask, since they obviously prefer not to meet with you
Say you've noticed the cancellations, ask what is in the way, and agree a slot that works

rubric: Name the pattern, ask about the cause and agree a workable arrangement.
Distractors drop the practice, avoid the issue or escalate prematurely.

items.prompt: Two reports disagree about who owns a shared task, and the work is slowing. What is the best first step?

options.label: Tell them to sort it out between themselves and step in only if the deadline slips
Reassign the task to a third person so that neither side feels they have lost out
Hear each person separately, then bring them together to agree ownership against team goals
Decide on your own who owns it and announce it in the team channel to end the debate quickly

rubric: Listening to both sides and then facilitating agreement against goals is the sound approach.
Distractors impose a decision, abdicate, or sidestep the conflict.

items.prompt: A report's error rate has risen over the last month. What should you do first?

options.label: Add it to the next formal performance review so it is handled together with the rest of their record
Remind the whole team in a meeting about quality standards, without naming anyone, so nobody feels singled out
Meet privately, share specific examples, and check whether expectations or obstacles explain the change
Quietly reassign their harder work to others until the error rate comes back down, avoiding an awkward talk

rubric: Address it early and privately with evidence and curiosity about causes.
Distractors delay, work around the person, or give vague group messages.

items.prompt: A new report starts on Monday. Which actions would you take in their first weeks? Select all that apply.

options.label: Introduce them to key colleagues and name a buddy
Leave them to find their own way so they learn independence
Agree what success looks like for the first 30 days
Set up a recurring one-on-one and use the first to learn their goals
Wait three months before giving any feedback to see their natural style

rubric: Onboarding needs clear expectations, a regular one-on-one and connections.
Leaving them alone or withholding feedback delays learning and leaves them guessing.

items.prompt: You delegated a client report to Ravi, due Friday. On Wednesday he tells you he is only a third done because he is waiting on data from another team. What is your best next step?

options.label: Tell him the deadline is fixed and he must work extra hours to make it, whatever the cause of the delay
Ask what is blocking him, help get the data, and confirm what remains his to deliver
Extend the deadline for him silently and say nothing to the client until Friday arrives, hoping it works out
Take the report back and finish it yourself so that the client deadline is definitely safe and no one is blamed

rubric: Remove the obstacle while keeping ownership with Ravi.
Distractors reverse the delegation, ignore the real cause, or hide the risk.

items.prompt: You delegate a monthly vendor report to Priya, who has never produced it. You want it done well without doing it yourself. Which delegation approach fits best?

options.label: Keep the report yourself and have her watch you produce it twice more, so she sees every detail first
Assign it with only a deadline, since checking in would signal that you don't trust her skills
Hand over last month's file and ask her to figure it out, so she learns by discovery
Define the outcome and deadline, walk through the first one together, and set a mid-point check

rubric: A first-time task needs a clear outcome, some support and a planned check-in.
Distractors confuse hands-off delegation with trust or replace delegation with observation.

items.prompt: In a one-on-one, your report Tom says "all fine" to every question and offers no topics. What should you do next?

options.label: Accept that all is fine and end the meeting early to respect his time and workload
Ask a specific open question, such as what took more effort than expected this week
Ask directly whether he is unhappy with you, so any real issue comes out quickly
Switch to reviewing your own list of task updates so the meeting time is still used

rubric: Specific open questions give a quiet report an easy way into real topics.
Distractors end the conversation, turn it into a status check, or put him on the spot.

items.prompt: You want to give feedback using the Situation-Behaviour-Impact model. Which statement applies it correctly?

options.label: In meetings you tend to be rude, so I'd like you to be more respectful with your colleagues from now on
You are generally dismissive in meetings, which makes people feel that you don't value their ideas
In Tuesday's client call, you cut Sam off twice, and the client then missed the figures Sam was about to share
Several people mentioned that you interrupt, so you should work on your listening in client calls

rubric: It names a specific situation, an observable behaviour and a concrete impact.
Distractors use labels, generalisations or second-hand reports instead of observed behaviour.

items.prompt: You told a report to "be more proactive". Which rewrite turns this into a clear, checkable expectation?

options.label: Be visible in team discussions and volunteer for tasks more often, where your workload allows it
Flag any risk to a deadline in the team channel two days before it is due, with a proposed fix
Show more initiative on projects and take ownership whenever you see a gap in the team's work
Think ahead about problems and speak up early, so that the team is not surprised by any delays

rubric: It states an observable action, a timing and an output that can be checked.
Distractors restate the vague trait in different words without a measurable behaviour.

items.prompt: Two stakeholders each ask your analyst, Mei, for urgent work this week. She has capacity for only one request. What should you do?

options.label: Ask her to split her time evenly so that neither stakeholder feels let down by the team this week
Tell her to do whichever request arrived first, since order of arrival is a neutral and fair rule
Weigh both against team priorities, agree the order with the stakeholders, then tell her the outcome
Let her negotiate with both stakeholders directly, so that she builds her influence skills over time

rubric: Prioritising conflicting demands is the manager's job; she shouldn't have to arbitrate.
Distractors use arbitrary rules, dilute the work, or push the conflict onto her.

items.prompt: You are delegating an unfamiliar task to a team member. Which items belong in your delegation brief? Select all that apply.

options.label: A step-by-step method they must follow exactly, even if they know a better one
When and how you will check progress
The outcome you expect and the deadline
Which decisions they can make alone and which need you
A note that you may quietly redo parts you don't like

rubric: A good brief covers outcome, deadline, decision authority and check-ins.
Prescribing every step or secretly redoing work undermines ownership and trust.

items.prompt: Dev has missed his second deadline this month. Both times the work was good but late, and you have only mentioned it in passing before. You have a one-on-one tomorrow. What is the best next step?

options.label: Issue a written warning now, because two missed deadlines in a single month is enough to show a pattern
Meet privately to name the pattern, ask what is behind the delays, and agree a specific plan
Quietly move his deadlines onto a teammate so that the team's overall output is not affected by him
Raise it at the team meeting to set a shared standard on deadlines without singling out any one person

rubric: A private conversation naming the pattern and finding the cause comes before formal steps.
Distractors escalate too early, avoid the issue, or address it publicly.

items.prompt: Mia was a strong performer for a year. Since she took on a new product area with no training, her work quality has dropped. She is still keen and works the same hours. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: A skill gap from the new product area, since her effort is unchanged and the drop began with the change
A role-fit problem, since a year of strong results shows the job no longer challenges her enough
A motivation problem, since people who stop asking questions have usually lost interest in their work
A workload problem, since any quality drop in a strong performer comes from too many tasks at once

rubric: The timing and unchanged effort point to a skill gap, not a will problem.
Distractors jump to motivation, workload or fit without evidence.

items.prompt: A manager often reschedules one-on-ones. Later the team says they rarely raise problems early. Which analysis best links the two?

options.label: The team has no problems worth raising, since nothing has been escalated to senior leaders recently
One-on-ones are too frequent, so staff run out of topics and would be better served by fewer meetings
The team lacks the maturity to raise problems and needs training on speaking up in meetings
Repeated cancellations signal that their issues rank below other work, so they stop saving topics for you

rubric: Cancelled meetings signal low priority, which reduces candour and early warnings.
Distractors blame the team or read silence as the absence of problems.

items.prompt: Ana and Leo clash repeatedly. Each time, the dispute is over who gets the final say on client emails. They are otherwise friendly and work well together. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Personality incompatibility, since the clashes repeat and always involve the same two people
Unclear decision rights, since the disputes always arise around the same approval step
Competition for recognition, since approving emails gives one person more visible authority than the other
Poor communication skills, since both of them could explain their views more calmly to each other

rubric: Conflicts that cluster around one step and ease elsewhere point to unclear roles.
Distractors blame personalities or skills despite their otherwise good working relationship.

items.prompt: You asked a report to "do a competitor analysis". It came back thorough but covered the wrong competitors and missed what you needed for a pricing decision. Which step in the process failed?

options.label: The employee should have asked more questions, since checking scope is the report's responsibility alone
The task went to the wrong person, since an experienced analyst would never have misjudged the scope
The brief named a task but not the decision it would inform, so scope and depth were guesses
The deadline was too generous, since extra time always lets the scope drift away from the real need

rubric: Without the purpose, the report could not judge scope; the failure was in the brief.
Distractors blame the employee, the person chosen or the deadline instead of the missing purpose.

items.prompt: Sam, your top performer, now works late, is curt in meetings and has not taken leave for months. His output is still the highest on the team. Which reading is best supported?

options.label: Early burnout risk, since high output can mask strain that shows first in behaviour and habits
A conflict with peers, since irritability in meetings usually points to one specific colleague
Healthy commitment, since sustained high output shows the workload is manageable for him
A career-growth issue, since top performers who work late are mostly seeking promotion

rubric: Changes in behaviour and habits are early burnout signals that output can hide.
Distractors read output as proof of wellbeing or assume a single unsupported cause.

items.prompt: Decisions on your team have become slow. Which observations suggest your own micromanagement is a cause? Select all that apply.

options.label: A new hire asks many questions in the first week
Two engineers take a week to settle a genuine technical disagreement
Reports have stopped proposing solutions and now wait for you to say what to do
Routine drafts wait in your inbox for review before anything goes out
Staff ask your approval for small choices that are within their remit

rubric: Approval-seeking, review bottlenecks and learned passivity all trace back to manager control.
A real technical disagreement and a new hire's questions are normal and unrelated.

items.prompt: Your weekly team update lists five goals. Yet a survey says "priorities are unclear", and when a client issue hit, two reports worked on different goals. What is the most likely underlying cause?

options.label: Five goals is too few, since a longer list would have covered the client work that interrupted
The goals are shared but not ranked, so people can't tell what yields when demands collide
The team doesn't read updates, so the weekly message should be moved into a meeting instead
Two reports are underperforming, since clear priorities are always understood by capable staff

rubric: A list without ranking leaves people to guess trade-offs when demands conflict.
Distractors blame the channel, individuals or the number of goals rather than missing prioritisation.

items.prompt: A previously reliable report now misses deadlines. You need to separate a motivation problem from a skill problem. Which observation most strongly points to a motivation problem?

options.label: He finishes self-picked tasks quickly but stalls on assigned tasks of equal difficulty
He makes more errors on tasks that use the new tooling rolled out last month, and the errors are mostly in steps he has not been trained on
His output fell right after a new approval step was added to the team workflow
He asks frequent clarifying questions on work that differs from his past projects

rubric: Equal-difficulty tasks finished when self-chosen but not when assigned point to willingness, not capability.
The distractors describe skill gaps or process friction, which would affect effort-neutral performance.

items.prompt: Two reports keep clashing in planning meetings. Which observation most strongly suggests the cause is structural rather than a personality problem?

options.label: The dispute recurs whenever their separate targets compete for the same shared resource, even when relations are good
They clash more when one of them is tired or has had a stressful week outside of work, and the tension fades once they recover
They have different working styles, with one planning far ahead and the other improvising, so each reads the other's approach as careless
Each one describes the other's tone in meetings as dismissive and says it happens in most interactions

rubric: A conflict that recurs when goals compete for one resource is driven by the structure of the work, not by the individuals.
Tone, mood and style differences are personal explanations that learners overweight.

items.prompt: You delegated a monthly analysis to a capable report. It arrived on time and complete, but in the wrong format and at the wrong depth, and it was reworked three times. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Success criteria for format and depth were never stated at handoff
The deadline was too tight for the report to ask any questions
The report lacks the motivation to take ownership of recurring work
The report was not given enough authority to make decisions

rubric: Complete, on-time work that misses format and depth points to unstated expectations at delegation.
Motivation, time pressure and authority explanations do not fit work that was complete and on time.

items.prompt: You review notes from six months of one-on-ones with each of your reports. Which pattern most clearly shows the meetings are not supporting development?

options.label: Meetings are often moved by a day or two when deadlines get tight, but they always happen within the week
Reports often bring personal topics, and you spend part of the meeting listening without steering back to work
Meetings often end ten minutes early because the reports have already covered their agenda items with you
Every meeting is spent on ticket status; career, feedback and obstacles never come up

rubric: A status-only pattern across months means the meeting works as a progress report, with no development content.
The distractors are normal variations that don't show a development gap.

items.prompt: A report gets glowing peer feedback for being helpful, yet misses most of her own goals. Which explanation best accounts for the gap between the two views?

options.label: Peers see her visible helpfulness, while her own goals measure delivery, so she may be trading goals for favours
Peers see her day-to-day work more closely than you do, so their view is the better guide and the goals are likely wrong
Peers are softening their ratings to avoid friction with a colleague, so the feedback tells you little about her work
Her goals were probably set too high for her role, so her results look weak when her real output is solid

rubric: The two sources measure different things: visible helpfulness versus delivery on her own objectives.
The distractors dismiss one source entirely rather than analysing what each measures.

items.prompt: Decisions on your team have become slow. Which observations suggest micromanagement is a cause? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reports stopped proposing options and ask what the manager wants
Reports ask for approval on cheap, reversible decisions
The team disagrees openly in planning meetings
Decisions often wait for a slot in the manager's calendar
Decisions are recorded in a shared log after being made

rubric: Seeking approval on reversible choices, waiting on the manager's calendar and reports no longer proposing options all show decisions routed through the manager.
Logging decisions and open disagreement are signs of a healthy team, not of control.

items.prompt: A colleague on your team left two months ago, and Priya absorbed part of her work. Her quality has dropped and she answers "fine" when asked. You want the cause before acting. Which step best reveals it?

options.label: Ask her peers what they have noticed about her focus, attitude and effort since the colleague left
Open a formal improvement plan so the expectations are written down and clear
Reassign the inherited work immediately and see whether her quality recovers by itself
Compare her workload and hours before and after the departure with quality on her tasks

rubric: Comparing load and hours with quality on retained tasks tests overload against other causes.
Peer gossip, a formal plan or reassignment skip the diagnosis and risk acting on a wrong cause.

items.prompt: A high-stakes client report is due in five days. Sam is capable but new to this client, and you also want to develop him. Criteria: protect the client, build his skill, keep your time modest. Which approach is best?

options.label: Give Sam only the easy sections without client context, so any mistakes stay small and you rewrite the rest
Give Sam the whole report and stay out of it until delivery, so he has full ownership of the result
Give Sam the full report with stated quality criteria and a midweek draft review
Write it yourself and walk Sam through the finished report afterwards, so the client gets a safe result

rubric: Clear criteria plus one draft checkpoint protects the client and develops Sam at low cost to your time.
Zero oversight risks the client, doing it yourself prevents development, and a trimmed task withholds context.

items.prompt: A report was curt with a client this morning. Criteria: the feedback must be specific, timely and preserve the working relationship. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Hold it for the quarterly review so it can be put in context alongside her other feedback from the period
Raise it today in private, describe what you saw and its impact, then ask for her view
Start with praise, mention the issue briefly, and finish with more praise so she stays motivated
Correct her in the team channel so the whole team learns what the client standard is

rubric: Private, same-day, behaviour-and-impact feedback with an invitation to respond meets all three criteria.
Delay loses timeliness, public correction damages the relationship, and a praise sandwich buries specifics.

items.prompt: A report's output has been below the bar for two months. Criteria: fairness, a real chance to improve, and a record if the situation escalates. Which response is best?

options.label: Wait for the annual review so that the feedback has a full year of data behind it and can be compared with the rest of the team
Set expectations in writing, agree a timeline with support, and hold regular check-ins before any formal step
Put them on a formal improvement plan now so that the record exists as early as possible and they know how serious it is
Move their hardest tasks to others quietly so that team results do not suffer while you watch whether their output recovers

rubric: Written expectations, support and check-ins give a fair chance and build a record.
Jumping to a formal plan, waiting a year, or quietly removing work each fail on fairness or chance to improve.

items.prompt: You manage nine reports and can spend about five hours a week on one-on-ones. Criteria: everyone gets regular time, new hires get extra support, and the schedule is sustainable. Which cadence is best?

options.label: Meet weekly for thirty minutes only with reports who are struggling, and skip the rest unless they ask for time
Every report gets thirty minutes every two weeks, and the two newest hires get thirty minutes weekly
Every report gets forty-five minutes weekly, which treats everyone equally and uses all of the available time
Hold one-on-ones only when a report asks for one, so that your time goes where it is most wanted and needed

rubric: Biweekly for all with weekly for new hires fits within the budget and gives extra support where needed.
An hour weekly for nine exceeds the time, and ad hoc or struggle-only schedules leave quiet reports without support.

items.prompt: Two reports tell you privately that a third often talks over them in meetings. Criteria: stop the behaviour, be fair to all three, and avoid exposing the two who came to you. Which response is best?

options.label: Wait a month to see whether the behaviour continues before saying anything to anyone
Raise it in the next team meeting as a general reminder that everyone should let colleagues finish speaking
Observe a meeting, then give the colleague specific private feedback and follow up
Ask the two reports to raise it directly with their colleague and tell you how the conversation goes

rubric: Observing first, then giving private, specific feedback and following up stops the behaviour without exposing the reporters.
A general reminder is ignored, shifting the work to the reporters puts the burden on them, and waiting lets harm continue.

items.prompt: You are judging whether a report is ready for promotion. Which criteria are sound to apply? Select all that apply.

options.label: How likely the person is to leave if refused
The same bar applied to every report on the team
Sustained performance at the scope of the next level
Evidence from several sources, not only your impression
Time served in the current role

rubric: Sustained next-level performance, multiple evidence sources and a consistent bar make the decision fair and defensible.
Tenure and flight risk say nothing about readiness and bias the decision.

items.prompt: You have one stretch project. Ana is your top performer and already has several visible projects. Ben is steady, wants to build exactly this skill, and carries moderate delivery risk. Criteria: grow the team's capability, keep delivery risk acceptable, and give fair access to opportunities. Which choice is best?

options.label: Give it to whoever has more seniority, since that is the simplest rule to explain to the team
Give it to Ben with defined support and checkpoints, and find Ana a different growth opportunity
Split it evenly between Ana and Ben with no single owner so that both can share the credit
Give it to Ana because she is the lowest delivery risk and the result is most predictable

rubric: Ben's development goal, bounded risk via checkpoints, and a separate opportunity for Ana satisfy all three criteria.
Defaulting to Ana concentrates opportunities, shared ownership blurs accountability, and seniority ignores development needs.

items.prompt: A high-visibility client deliverable is due in two weeks. Your senior analyst could do it flawlessly but is at capacity. A mid-level analyst wants stretch work but has never led one. Criteria: fixed deadline, client-ready quality, development valued. What is the best choice?

options.label: Give it to the mid-level analyst and stay hands-off so she owns the outcome fully, stepping in only if she asks
Give it to the mid-level analyst with scoped milestones, early reviews, and a pre-agreed trigger for you to step in
Give it to the senior analyst and clear her other work, since a missed deadline costs far more than slower development
Split it evenly between both so the senior can quietly fix problems while the junior is credited for the whole piece

rubric: Checkpoints and a stated trigger meet the quality, deadline and development criteria together.
Distractors trade away one criterion or confuse hands-off delegation with ownership.

items.prompt: A manager's weekly 30-minute one-on-ones are all project status. Reports call them useful, but nobody raises career topics or concerns. Criteria: keep visibility, surface risks early, support growth, add no meeting time. Which change is best?

options.label: Keep status as the main agenda and add a career question in the last two minutes, since status updates need live discussion
Add a second weekly meeting for career talk so status keeps its slot and growth gets separate dedicated time
Move status to an async tracker and give the meeting to the report's agenda, blockers and growth
Cut one-on-ones to monthly because status is covered elsewhere, leaving reports to raise concerns as they arise

rubric: Moving status async frees time for the topics that surface risk and growth without adding meetings.
Distractors keep status dominant, reduce contact, or break the no-extra-time criterion.

items.prompt: Your top salesperson hits 140% of quota but interrupts and belittles peers in meetings, and two peers have hinted they may leave. Criteria: protect team retention, treat her fairly, preserve results. What is the best first move?

options.label: Move her to solo accounts to separate her from peers, which protects the team without a difficult conversation
Ask the affected peers to confront her directly, since feedback from colleagues lands harder than from a manager
Give her specific behaviour-and-impact feedback now, state the expected standard, and set a date to review change
Wait until the annual review so the feedback can be framed alongside her results and compensation in context

rubric: Prompt, specific feedback with a follow-up addresses retention risk and is fair while keeping her output.
Distractors delay, avoid the conversation, or shift the manager's duty onto peers.

items.prompt: You have a fixed 3% raise pool for six reports. Two high performers have active outside offers; the others are solid. Criteria: retain critical talent, perceived fairness, stay within budget. Which approach is best?

options.label: Give the two flight risks the whole pool and nothing to the others, since retention risk outweighs everything else
Let reports submit cases for raises and fund the most persuasive, so the process feels open and merit-based
Weight raises by documented contribution and market risk, and explain the criteria without sharing individual figures
Split the pool equally at 3% each, since uniform treatment is the only way to avoid resentment on the team

rubric: Differentiating on stated criteria retains key people while keeping the process defensible.
Distractors ignore retention, ignore fairness, or reward persuasion rather than contribution.

items.prompt: Standard advice says to give feedback immediately. A report's launch failed an hour ago and she is visibly shaken. Criteria: she can absorb it, the learning isn't lost, trust is kept. Which approach is best?

options.label: Acknowledge the setback and offer support now, then hold a structured debrief within a day or two
Send written feedback tonight so she can read it privately and respond whenever she feels ready to
Say nothing until her next scheduled review so emotions settle and feedback joins other performance topics
Deliver the full critique now while details are fresh, since delay weakens the lesson and signals avoidance

rubric: A short delay keeps the lesson fresh while letting her absorb it and preserves trust.
Distractors apply the rule rigidly, delay too long, or remove the conversation.

items.prompt: A manager plans a 30-day PIP for a report who has never received documented feedback. The only goal written is 'improve communication'. Which concerns about this plan are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Any PIP should run for a year so the report has time to rebuild habits fully and prove consistency
Earlier expectations and feedback were never documented, so the PIP may feel like a surprise and look unfair
No coaching or check-in dates are stated, so the plan tests the report without offering any support
A PIP should never involve HR, because involving them turns a coaching conversation into a legal one
'Improve communication' has no observable measure, so success or failure cannot be judged fairly

rubric: Valid concerns are missing prior documentation, unmeasurable goals, and no support built in.
HR-avoidance and year-long duration are overgeneralised ideas that don't address fairness of this plan.

items.prompt: Dan and Lee keep clashing over who owns the release process, and each has escalated to you twice this month. You are going on leave soon and want clear ownership without becoming a bottleneck. Which response best meets those criteria?

options.label: Tell them to sort it out themselves while you're away, so they build conflict skills without your interference
Split the process in half so each owns a part, which removes the overlap without anyone feeling they lost
Facilitate a session to agree decision rights and escalation rules, document them, then step back and check in
Decide today who owns it and announce it, since a fast and clear ruling ends the clash before you leave

rubric: Co-created, documented decision rights give lasting clarity and remove you from the loop.
Distractors create a bottleneck, abandon the problem, or split work without resolving decision authority.

items.prompt: Design an onboarding plan for a remote hire. Constraints: you have 3 hours a week, a first real deliverable is due by day 30, the hire needs context from four teams, and your working hours overlap only partly. Which plan meets all constraints?

options.label: Daily 45-minute 1:1s with you for the first month, with goals shared at day 30 once you see how they work
A written handbook and recorded videos, with a single check-in at day 30 to review goals and the deliverable
A full first week of live meetings with all four teams, then goals and the deliverable set once context is built
Weekly 1:1s, 30/60/90 goals with a day-30 deliverable, an assigned buddy, and async intros to the four teams

rubric: It fits the time budget, sets the day-30 goal early, and uses buddy and async methods for context and timezones.
Distractors exceed the time budget, delay goals, or leave the hire without regular support.

items.prompt: Design expectations for support engineers. Constraints: reflect customer outcomes, resist gaming, and stay fair when ticket difficulty varies across engineers. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Use a balanced set of resolution quality, satisfaction and reopen rate, reviewed with context on ticket mix
Use resolution quality and reopen rate only, compared against one team-wide target so every engineer is held to one standard
Use satisfaction scores plus handle time, with the team average as the target and bonuses for engineers who beat it each month
Use tickets closed weighted by priority, ranked weekly and published, so output is transparent and easy to compare across the team

rubric: Balanced measures with context on difficulty resist gaming and keep comparisons fair.
Single-metric options invite gaming or ignore ticket difficulty.

items.prompt: After a reorganisation, your team is anxious. Constraints: you cannot reveal confidential details, you cannot promise job security, and you must restore trust within a month. Which plan fits?

options.label: Wait to speak until every detail is final, so nothing said later contradicts it and your credibility stays intact
Share what is known and unknown, set dates for updates, and invite questions within the limits you have
Redirect all questions to HR and leadership, so the team gets consistent official answers and you avoid error
Reassure everyone their jobs are safe, since visible certainty calms people faster than caveats about what is still undecided

rubric: Honest known/unknown updates on a fixed cadence build trust within the constraints.
Distractors stay silent, promise what you can't guarantee, or deflect.

items.prompt: You will move teams in four months and want Sam, a strong individual contributor, to succeed you without disrupting delivery. Which transition plan best fits?

options.label: Phase duties in from meetings and one-on-ones with coaching, set review points, and agree a handover date
Keep the management duties until your last fortnight, then hand them over with a written guide and be reachable for questions
Hand Sam the management duties next week so the four months act as a trial, with you as the safety net throughout
Announce Sam as successor and train mainly through shadowing you, so delivery is untouched until the final weeks

rubric: A phased handover with coaching and review points builds skill while protecting delivery.
Distractors are too abrupt, passive, or too late to develop a successor.

items.prompt: Design a feedback routine for a six-person remote team across timezones. Constraints: feedback to each person at least every two weeks, no extra all-hands meetings, no public criticism, at most 90 minutes of your time weekly. Which design fits?

options.label: Ad hoc feedback by direct message when issues arise, so nothing is delayed by waiting for a meeting
A quarterly 360 review across the team with a written summary, so feedback is thorough and well evidenced
Weekly team retros where each member gets feedback aloud from peers, for transparency and equal treatment
Biweekly 1:1s with a standing feedback segment, brief written praise in the team channel, corrections kept private

rubric: It guarantees the biweekly cadence, keeps criticism private, and fits the time limit.
Distractors add meetings, publicise criticism, or fail the cadence requirement.

items.prompt: You are redesigning one-on-ones for 8 reports. Constraints: the report owns the agenda, you have 4 hours a week for this, and performance, development and wellbeing must each be covered monthly. Which elements fit? Select all that apply.

options.label: A manager-written fixed agenda used for every report, so coverage is consistent and nothing is missed
Weekly 60-minute meetings with every report, so there is ample space for every topic each time
A monthly rotating prompt on development or wellbeing slotted into a 30-minute biweekly or weekly meeting
A shared running doc where the report adds topics beforehand and both record actions
Skipping meetings when a report has no topics, with no other contact until the next scheduled period

rubric: A report-owned doc plus rotating monthly prompts keep ownership, coverage and the time budget.
The fixed agenda removes ownership, skipping loses coverage, and weekly hour-long meetings need 8 hours.

items.prompt: Priya tells you she is exhausted; her workload has grown for months. Your draft plan: reassign two of her tasks to a colleague and encourage her to take leave. A peer reviews it and says something important is missing. What is it?

options.label: A review of why her workload grew and a priorities and scope reset with her, so overload doesn't return
A team announcement about her situation, so colleagues understand why tasks are moving and offer help
A written warning recording that she raised workload late, protecting you if her performance falls further
A pay review for the extra hours she has worked, because compensation is the main cause of burnout

rubric: The plan treats symptoms; without addressing the cause of the growth, overload will recur.
Distractors breach trust, expose her privacy, or assume pay is the root cause.
